t.2.49.1: Having spent the night there, the two princes, subduers of their enemies, saluted the great sage and then set out toward that mountain.
t.2.49.2: Seeing them setting out, he followed them as a father follows his sons. Then the great sage began to speak these words.
t.2.49.3: Then, having reached the Kālindī, the swift-flowing river, you must build a raft there and cross the Aṃśumatī river.
t.2.49.4: Then, reaching a great banyan tree with green leaves, dark in hue, grown vast amid many trees and frequented by Siddhas,
t.2.49.6: "That path to Citrakūṭa has been travelled by me very many times; it is lovely and gentle, and free from forest fires." Having thus described the path, the great sage turned back.
t.2.49.5: Then, having gone just a krośa further, O Rāma, you will see a dark-blue forest, mingled with palāśa and jujube trees and with the bamboos of the Yamunā.
t.2.49.7: When that sage had returned, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "We have indeed done meritorious deeds, O Saumitri, since the sage shows compassion to us."
t.2.49.8: Having thus taken counsel together, those two high-minded tigers among men, placing Sītā in front, went to the river Kālindī.
t.2.49.9: Then the two of them made a very large raft by binding logs together, and Lakṣmaṇa, cutting reeds and branches, made a comfortable seat for Sītā.
t.2.49.10: There Rāma, son of Daśaratha, helped his beloved, who was like Śrī herself beyond all imagining and slightly abashed, to climb aboard the boat.
t.2.49.11: Then, on a raft, they crossed the river Yamunā, Aṃśumatī, swift-flowing and garlanded with waves, by means of the many trees growing on its banks.
t.2.49.12: Having crossed over, they abandoned the raft and, setting out from the forest by the Yamunā, reached the dark nyagrodha tree, cool and with green leaves.
t.2.49.13: "May I see Kausalyā, and the illustrious Sumitrā as well!" So saying, Sītā joined her palms in reverence and walked around the great tree.
t.2.49.14: Then, having gone the distance of just a krośa, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa killed many deer fit for sacrifice and roamed about in the forest by the Yamunā.
t.2.49.15: Having roamed through the lovely forest that resounded with flocks of peacocks and teemed with elephants and monkeys, they, of undejected appearance, reached a level stretch of riverbank and came to an agreeable dwelling place.
